summary: Defines LEDBAT, an experimental congestion control algorithm for background traffic. It watches changes in one-way delay to detect queues building up, and uses spare bandwidth while backing off quickly so it does not slow down other traffic on the path.

eli5.summary: Like a polite person on a crowded sidewalk who walks fast when there is room but steps aside the moment others show up.

questions: how does delay based congestion control work
how to run background transfers without slowing other traffic
what is the ledbat target delay
how does ledbat differ from tcp congestion control
subtitle: A congestion control scheme that lets background transfers use spare bandwidth and step aside when other traffic shows up.

tldr.problem: Background transfers such as software updates and file sharing should not slow down interactive traffic, but standard TCP congestion control may be too aggressive for them.
tldr.mechanism: A LEDBAT sender measures one-way delay, treats growth in queueing delay as an early sign of congestion, and adjusts its congestion window in proportion to how far the delay is from a target of 100 milliseconds or less.
tldr.outcome: LEDBAT uses spare capacity yet yields quickly to competing flows, and in the worst case it is no more aggressive than standard TCP. The RFC is Experimental.

facts.label: Response to loss
facts.value: Halve cwnd, at most once per RTT

today: RFC 6817 is an Experimental specification, published in December 2012, and it has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata. The RFC itself lists several areas that still needed experimentation, including parameter values, filters and network effects.

sections.title: Background Traffic and Its Goals
sections.content:
RFC 5681 TCP congestion control tries to share a bottleneck link fairly among all flows. That is not what a software update or a file-sharing program wants. These background applications want to stay out of the way of foreground applications that are sensitive to delay or bandwidth.

LEDBAT is an experimental delay-based congestion control mechanism with three goals: use the available bandwidth and keep queueing delay low when no other traffic is present, add only limited queueing delay to what other flows already cause, and yield quickly to standard TCP flows on the same bottleneck. Unlike delay-based schemes such as TCP Vegas, which aim for more throughput than TCP, LEDBAT is a scavenger that is meant to be no more aggressive than TCP.
sections.eli5: Some downloads are not in a hurry. LEDBAT lets them use whatever road is empty and pull over when someone more important comes along.

sections.title: Where LEDBAT Applies
sections.content:
LEDBAT can be part of a transport protocol or of an application, provided the data path can carry timestamps and acknowledge data frequently. The RFC says it can be used with TCP, SCTP and DCCP (with extensions where needed), and with proprietary protocols built on UDP, such as peer-to-peer applications. It is expected to work well when a sender or receiver sits on a residential access network.

With an ECN-capable framing protocol, LEDBAT should treat an ECN mark as it would a loss. Queue management matters too: if Active Queue Management drops or marks packets before LEDBAT reacts, LEDBAT reverts to standard TCP behavior instead of yielding. Weighted Fair Queuing in a home gateway has a similar effect, but the RFC notes that both outcomes still match LEDBAT's goals.
sections.eli5: It works for many kinds of programs, as long as they can stamp each message with the time it was sent and get quick replies.

sections.title: How the Sender and Receiver Work
sections.content:
Each data segment carries a timestamp from the sender. The receiver subtracts that timestamp from its own clock to get the one-way delay and sends the value back in the next acknowledgement. A receiver MAY bundle several delay samples into one ACK, but MUST send them in the order generated.

The sender keeps a congestion window (cwnd). On each acknowledgement it updates a base delay (the minimum delay seen) and a current delay, and computes queuing_delay = current_delay - base_delay. It then computes off_target = (TARGET - queuing_delay) / TARGET and changes the window by GAIN * off_target * bytes_newly_acked * MSS / cwnd. When queueing delay is below the target the window grows; when it is above, the window shrinks.

On data loss the window is halved, at most once per round-trip time. If no ACKs arrive within a congestion timeout (CTO), the window drops to one MSS and the CTO doubles. A receiver MUST send at least one ACK in every round-trip time.
sections.eli5: Every message carries a clock reading. By checking how late messages arrive compared with the fastest ones, the sender can tell when a queue is building and slows down before anyone is hurt.

sections.title: Parameters and Delay Estimation
sections.content:
The base delay is the minimum delay observed, kept as one minimum per minute for the last BASE_HISTORY minutes, so that real route changes are eventually noticed. The current delay is smoothed by a FILTER(), which may be a NULL filter, an exponentially weighted moving average, or a MIN filter over a small window. The sender SHOULD use at least 4 delay samples per round-trip time unless the window is small.

  • TARGET MUST be 100 milliseconds or less. The RFC picks this because ITU-T G.114 treats 150 ms one-way delay as acceptable for most voice use, while a target that is too low makes the sender sensitive to noise.
  • GAIN MUST be 1 or less; a value of 1 limits ramp-up to the rate of TCP Reno in congestion avoidance.
  • ALLOWED_INCREASE SHOULD be 1 and MUST be greater than 0.
  • BASE_HISTORY SHOULD be 10.
  • INIT_CWND and MIN_CWND SHOULD both be 2, and MUST be no larger than the TCP values.

Clock offset between sender and receiver cancels out, because it affects the measured delay and the base delay equally. Clock skew does not cancel, and Appendix A suggests ways to correct for it.
sections.eli5: The sender remembers the fastest trip it has seen lately, and treats anything slower than that as waiting in line. It aims to add only a small wait of its own.

sections.title: Competing Flows and Fairness
sections.content:
LEDBAT is most aggressive when the queueing delay estimate is zero, and then it ramps up at the same rate as standard TCP. Because it reduces its rate earlier than TCP and always halves its window on loss, a LEDBAT flow whose delay estimates are completely wrong falls back to standard TCP behavior and is no more aggressive than TCP.

LEDBAT yields to high-load flows, but it may not yield to low-load, latency-sensitive traffic such as VoIP that causes no measurable queueing. The TARGET value caps the total extra delay all concurrent LEDBAT flows add.

Among LEDBAT flows themselves, the RFC admits there is no mechanism to equalize shares. A latecomer's advantage can arise: a new flow that starts while another LEDBAT flow holds the queue at the target may mistake that standing queue for base delay and build on top of it. The RFC argues that small gaps in real traffic usually let the latecomer measure the true base delay, and it does not recommend multiplicative decrease as a cure.
sections.eli5: If a newcomer shows up while the line is already long, it may think the line is normal and push ahead. Usually small pauses in traffic let it see the truth.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If an attacker or fault makes the delay estimates read as zero and sets TARGET to infinity, LEDBAT degrades to TCP-like behavior, so it is fundamentally limited to being as aggressive as standard TCP.

A man in the middle who changes queueing delay, timestamps or reported delays can make a LEDBAT flow back off when there is no congestion. A protocol using LEDBAT ought to authenticate at least the timestamp field in data packets and the delay field in ACKs. The RFC says LEDBAT is not known to add new privacy or integrity concerns and is compatible with IPsec and TLS/DTLS.
sections.eli5: A trickster who fiddles with the clock readings could make the sender slow down for no reason, so those readings should be protected.
